Messages.Body:
Greetings all
I have just been trolling the site for a response to this and all the
results contradict themselves. Basically, if i first strike someone to
steal their gun, then they, if having used the manuver from the gun,
cannot strike with it, because they no longer have it so they no longer
have a strike. OK all well and good, yet if i play a withering at first
strike, someone is still free to declare a strike that requires a
discipline. Why is this? If a strike with a gun is no longer allowable
because said gun is stolen/destroyed with first strike and therefore
not allowed to resolve, why is the disciplined strike allowed to
resolve? I understand that S:CE "trumps" first strike, no probs but why
dodge?, or anything else for that matter? If first stike only means it
resolves before other strikes then the gun should still work (my strike
is still x ranged damage) If in response to this you say "but i have
destroyed your gun therefore you cannot strike with it" then I would
respond in a similar situation with: "but i have destroyed your
discipline therefore your strike is illegal"

Help guys, this seems like a bit of a screw up in the rules
cheers
Michael

Messages.Author: Jozxyqk
Messages.Body:


A minion is only "using" a discipline when he *plays* the card. If I
play Entombment, I'm using Obtenebration. But during the Strike
*Resolution* phase, I'm not *using* Obtenebration anymore; the card,
which was already legally played, established an effect that's going
to happen.

But in order for a strike from a .44 magnum to resolve, the equipment
needs to be there during Strike Resolution, because "the gun deals 2R
damage" is the strike. If the source of the damage is no longer there,
the damage doesn't happen.

Does this make sense?

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1140963823.3...@p10g2000cwp.googlegroups.com>,

sutekh_23 <bec...@aapt.net.au> writes:
>Greetings all
>I have just been trolling the site for a response to this and all the
>results contradict themselves. Basically, if i first strike someone to
>steal their gun, then they, if having used the manuver from the gun,
>cannot strike with it, because they no longer have it so they no longer
>have a strike. OK all well and good, yet if i play a withering at first
>strike, someone is still free to declare a strike that requires a
>discipline.

No, they've already declared the strike using that discipline. All
strikes are chosen (whatever they might be) in one go, and then resolved
in the appropriate order.

Playing a card requires you have the discipline. Resolving a card that
has a delayed resolution doesn't mean that you still have to have the
discipline (or access to it). That's common across all cards. If you,
for instance, only have access to Obfuscate via Changeling Skin Mask and
then lose it in combat, but continue an Obfuscate action via e.g. Form
of Mist, you can still successfully resolve the action - even though you
don't have Obfuscate anymore.

<http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/9e7c09
bec2e12841> (LSJ replying to me, when I forgot the history and made a
mess of it all.)

The consistency here is across play vs resolve of cards. You meet the
requirements when you play the card.

Weapon strikes have a special bit written about them in the rules. This
is actually similar to the RTR I mention in the above link where if you
need a piece of equipment to take an action (e.g. the burn a location
action on a bomb) and you lose it, the action fizzles. There, the
equipment is an enabler and losing it before resolution causes a fizzle.

So, the consistency is there, it's just across different points to where
you're looking.

>I understand that S:CE "trumps" first strike, no probs but why
>dodge?,

Because that's what the designers did. Actually, it's somewhat involved
because the Jyhad wording of the rules was a little vague on this.

There are several points here, though.

- At no point have the Rules Team issued a rules correction on this
point.
- You might think that e.g. a Celerity card would have been printed in
the Jyhad set which was, for example, Strike: Dodge / As above,
with First Strike, if Dodge was intended to go at normal strike
level.
- The V:TES rules changed several basic rules and card texts (aggravated
damage, dropping paralyse, 2 strength became +1 strength on many
vampires etc.) without changing the rules on Dodge.

So, the answer is "designer intent".

As to why it hasn't been changed? Most rules are only changed if
there's a pressing reason for it. You could tinker with any number of
rules without breaking the game - which is why it's inadvisable to do
so. So, if Dodge beating First Strike made a large shift in the
intended power level of certain cards (such as the changes to aggravated
damage in V:TES did, hence it being different now from either Jyhad or
V:TES), or if the rule added lots of unnecessary complexity for little
benefit (as in Paralyse and the (D) rush between "contested" titles on
Princes and Archbishops in the original release of Sabbat), then the
rules would be dropped, rewritten or streamlined.

Since this has never been the case with Dodge beating First Strike (even
if it is unintuitive to some), it's never been changed. (It would be
similarly unintuitive the other way round to other people, by the way.)

>or anything else for that matter? If first stike only means it
>resolves before other strikes then the gun should still work (my strike
>is still x ranged damage) If in response to this you say "but i have
>destroyed your gun therefore you cannot strike with it" then I would
>respond in a similar situation with: "but i have destroyed your
>discipline therefore your strike is illegal"

Your strike is, because of specific rules, dependent on the presence of
the equipment, as other equipment generated effects can be similarly
dependent.

Because of a blanket (read "consistent") application of a rule on
discipline requirements being checked at play but not resolution, my
discipline strike isn't dependent in the same fashion.

--

Messages.Author: Chris Berger
Messages.Body:
James Coupe wrote:
>
> Playing a card requires you have the discipline. Resolving a card that
> has a delayed resolution doesn't mean that you still have to have the
> discipline (or access to it). That's common across all cards. If you,
> for instance, only have access to Obfuscate via Changeling Skin Mask and
> then lose it in combat, but continue an Obfuscate action via e.g. Form
> of Mist, you can still successfully resolve the action - even though you
> don't have Obfuscate anymore.
>

This is very odd. An action requires a discipline and a ready vampire.
If the vampire loses the discipline, the action continues, but if the
vampire is no longer ready, the action fails.

See:
http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/e147b20e15c9bde1

Umm... care to have a go at explaining that one, James? ;)

(BTW, I'm not arguing with the rest of your post - I think first-strike
works exactly as it should... now I just wish there was more
first-strike in the game)

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1140970031.7...@t39g2000cwt.googlegroups.com>,

Chris Berger <ark...@ugcs.caltech.edu> writes:
>This is very odd. An action requires a discipline and a ready vampire.
> If the vampire loses the discipline, the action continues, but if the
>vampire is no longer ready, the action fails.
>
>See:
>http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/e147b20e15c9bde1
>
>Umm... care to have a go at explaining that one, James? ;)

One explanation would be that the discipline requirement is not one on
the action, but one on playing the card.

As in <http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/
9e7c09bec2e12841>, the difference between requiring Obfuscate to play
the card and the action itself requiring Obfuscate (when it resolves) is
pointed at.

So if you fail to meet the requirements of an action when it would
resolve, it fizzles. But meeting the discipline requirement is one you
meet when playing the card, and does not apply to the action.

However, that conflicts with the wording of Orb of Ulain:

The ally with this equipment cannot be targeted by (D) actions
that require Auspex, Chimerstry, Dominate, Presence or
Serpentis.

This implies that the actions themselves do require disciplines, rather
than just the play of the card.

Another explanation, then, would be that while the action does require
the discipline, only the "Play / Resolve" check on disciplines is made,
and not some standing check on whether the minion still meets the
requirements of the action (such as being out of torpor).

An alternative avenue of explanation might be that entering torpor
simply causes actions to fizzle when they meet resolution (or
potentially immediately), though that doesn't follow on from the text of
the ruling you cite and would probably need to be a clarification or
ruling.

Alternatively again, actions that don't specify "May be played by a
vampire in torpor" (or whatever) are implicitly saying "(D) [This ready
minion....]" but such text is taken as read because it is only the
difference that is usually interesting. This would then fail in the
same way that Ambush fails if the target untaps during the action and,
as an extension of that, "(D) This ready Baali...." would fizzle if the
acting vampire stopped being a Baali somehow[0].

Without further clarification from LSJ when he gets back, however,
disciplines are not checked for at the end of an action but (some) other
criteria are checked.

[0] The answer to this question involves Malkavian Time Auction.[1]
During an action, a vampire goes to torpor (triggering a Fame) and
ousting the controller of a Clan Impersonation you have on your acting
vampire, whilst you continue the action using Form of Mist. One could
imagine that the opposing vampire was going to go to torpor but saved
himself with an Undead Persistence such that he goes to torpor after
combat (so you can Strike: Combat Ends with FoM) and then he goes to
torpor, his controller being ousted[2], and his controller controls your
Clan Impersonation[3].

[1] The answer to all stupid questions involves Malkavian Time Auction,
Madness Network or Form of Mist. Protean-wielding Malkavians have a lot
to answer for.

[2] Assuming that an oust happening to someone else isn't "sufficiently
disruptive" to interrupt a Form of Mist.

[3] Clan Impersonating to Baali FTW.

Messages.Author: CthuluKitty
Messages.Body:
> >I understand that S:CE "trumps" first strike, no probs but why
> >dodge?,
>
> Because that's what the designers did. Actually, it's somewhat involved
> because the Jyhad wording of the rules was a little vague on this.

Additionally, there's no timing involved in a dodge. A dodge cancels
all effects the opposing minion's strike applies to the dodging minion
regardless of when those effects resolve. Dodge also avoids secondary
effects from Strike:Combat Ends, such as the damage from superior
Catatonic Fear or the untap from basic Meld with the Land.

> - The V:TES rules changed several basic rules and card texts (aggravated
> damage, dropping paralyse, 2 strength became +1 strength on many
> vampires etc.) without changing the rules on Dodge.

I thought aggravated damage was changed back to the original Jyhad
rules--after a period of time where the first point both sent the
vampire to torpor and required him to burn blood to prevent
destruction. How are the rules different from the original printing?
On this point, it's worth noting that a friend I occasionally play with
is very unhappy with the way aggravated damage was re-ammended. The
way it works is slightly confusing, and the fact that at times
(whenever damage=B+1 where B is the amount of blood on the wounded
vampire) aggravated and normal damage do the exact same thing is a bit
odd. I wonder if this rule was specifically ammended because Pulled
Fangs (which used to inflict 1 aggravated) was being used to burn
vampires. Now that PF has been fixed, the rules could be switched back
to the original VTES version, but it's very unlikely that this will
happen.

Some designer insight would be interesting on this matter, but
unfortunately LSJ is only likely to respond with "the rules were
written as intended", which is far from helpful or interesting.

> So, the answer is "designer intent".

You know, I noticed this line just now--after writing the above
comment. That's irony if anything is.

> As to why it hasn't been changed? Most rules are only changed if

> there's a pressing reason for it. ...(as in Paralyse and the (D) rush between >"contested" titles on Princes and Archbishops in the original release of Sabbat), then

> the rules would be dropped, rewritten or streamlined.

Don't forget Close Quarters, a rule from the original Jyhad rulebook
that was literally never used on even one single card, even though
Storm Sewers had the exact same effect.

That's all for me.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1140974980.3...@i40g2000cwc.googlegroups.com>,

CthuluKitty <vtana...@riseup.net> writes:
>> - The V:TES rules changed several basic rules and card texts (aggravated
>> damage, dropping paralyse, 2 strength became +1 strength on many
>> vampires etc.) without changing the rules on Dodge.
>
>I thought aggravated damage was changed back to the original Jyhad
>rules--after a period of time where the first point both sent the
>vampire to torpor and required him to burn blood to prevent
>destruction. How are the rules different from the original printing?

The original rules were unclear on what happened when multiple points of
aggravated damage came from multiple sources. e.g. a Dawn Operation
causing aggravated damage in combat, with two separate sources - my hand
strike and my Wolf Companion.

The ambiguity led to an interpretation, sometimes known as packeting.
(A google search for "packet" or "packets" will probably turn up answers
as a result.) As with Dodge, it's arguable if this interpretation was
"correct", but it became the right way to play until V:TES was printed.

Under the packeting rules, the first point of aggravated damage from
each packet (separate source) caused you to go to torpor. If you had
three separate sources of aggravated damage for a point each, they all
sent you to torpor. Amongst other things, this meant that a plain
vanilla Ivory Bow could NEVER burn a vampire. Nor could Pulled Fangs.
Nor could a 1 strength hit with Sengir Dagger. And so on.

Under the V:TES rules, the point that sent you to torpor also caused you
to burn a blood (or burn the vampire). This meant that against an empty
vampire, Ivory Bow, Pulled Fangs etc. could burn you. This
significantly upped their utility on the power curve. Additionally,
only the first point (regardless of source) sent you to torpor, so an
Ivory Bow wielding Dawn Operation user with a Wolf Companion could burn
a vampire on 1 blood, for example. (2 points of agg damage. First
sends to torpor and burns a blood. Second burns the vampire.)

Under the re-worked rules, official since LSJ's rulings and then, later,
printed in Sabbat War, the packeting was removed from the Jyhad rules.
The first point of aggravated damage against a non-wounded vampire sends
them to torpor, causing them to not burn a blood in the process. Each
point after that causes them to burn a blood to prevent destruction.
So, being hit with a Wolf Companion who's doing aggravated damage and an
Ivory Bow shot can burn you - if you're on zero blood.

It's harder to burn a vampire than in the V:TES rules, but easier than
in the Jyhad rules.

I'm not entirely certain if either set of rules (Jyhad or V:TES) dealt
extensively with the concept of dealing with aggravated damage being
dealt to a vampire who is already in torpor and can't be arsed to check.
(Would it re-send them to torpor, even though they were already there,
or would it notice etc.) There may be another quirk there.

Bottom line is: in Jyhad, you really wanted 2 agg damage from one source
to burn a vampire outright. This was what Flamethrower was for. In
V:TES, you could do it if the vampire was empty and you had a single
point. In the current rules, you need X+2 damage (at least one of which
is aggravated) if the vampire is not in, or on their way to, torpor
already.

>On this point, it's worth noting that a friend I occasionally play with
>is very unhappy with the way aggravated damage was re-ammended. The
>way it works is slightly confusing, and the fact that at times
>(whenever damage=B+1 where B is the amount of blood on the wounded
>vampire) aggravated and normal damage do the exact same thing is a bit
>odd.

It's a little odd, but lots of things in the game are a bit quirky
around the edge cases like that. The thing is, you know what these are
most of the time - here, it's pretty easy to work out, for example - and
plan to not run into them as best you can.

To be honest, I'd quite like to see 5 normal damage be slightly weaker
(somehow) than 5 aggravated damage in the situation you describe, but
there isn't a useful halfway house between the current rules and the
V:TES rules that I've ever been able to find. (If you can find one,
please feel free!)

Corner-case situation: Regenerative Blood doesn't help you against
aggravated damage but doesn't against normal damage, and Brother's Blood
can't stop a vampire from going to torpor because the first point of
aggravated damage is neither healed nor burned to prevent destruction.
But then, Sword of Nuln doesn't help you when it comes to aggravated
damage (because aggravated damage isn't healed), so there's up and
downs.

So yes, in principle, I sympathise. In practise, I can't see a useful
alteration that wouldn't either be tinkering for the sake of it or
unnecessarily complex.

>I wonder if this rule was specifically ammended because Pulled
>Fangs (which used to inflict 1 aggravated) was being used to burn
>vampires. Now that PF has been fixed, the rules could be switched back
>to the original VTES version, but it's very unlikely that this will
>happen.

No.

No-one, least of all me, would deny that Pulled Fangs was a powerful
card at the time, or would claim that it wasn't one of the reasons why
people looked at aggravated damage and said "Hmmm, that's a bit awkward
isn't it?"

However, the rules on aggravated damage and the text fix to Pulled Fangs
were made *at the same time*.

http://www.thelasombra.com/rules/RTR7-7.htm

The generally accepted wisdom these days goes along these lines:

- Aggravated damage in general was too good in V:TES. Whether packeting
existed or not in Jyhad, an Ivory Bow on its own couldn't burn a
vampire. Nor could Igo with a claw card on an empty Justicar.

- On top of that, Pulled Fangs was too good anyway. It gave free
aggravated damage, and could stack. With enough copies, you
could burn anyone. So it was toned down. From
http://www.white-wolf.com/VTES/migration.html, I believe that
the "doesn't stack" came in SW, though the change to aggravated
damage came with the 7/7 rulings.

I'd also note that there was a general problem game-wise at the time in
that a number of pro-strategies (those that help you win) were quite
awkwardly powerful, when their counterpart defensive strategies (those
that stop you being ousted / run over by a deck) were a bit rubbish.
Specifically, Return to Innocence made horrendous bleedzooka decks
possible, and Thoughts Betrayed made combat defence nigh-on impossible
against determined opposition. (Horribly aggressive vote was sort of
nuked with the Tomb re-write, but also needed Legacy of Pander to be
dealt with to complete the set.) And there was essentially a global
nuke across a range of rules facets *and* cards, to tone down a lot of
strategies.

Most such strategies are still viable, but aren't as outright powerful
now. Thus giving rise to an environment where a slightly fragile Choir
deck can still do well without getting a Tomb of Rameses Arika Soul Gem,
Freak Drive, Return to Innocence up its ass second turn. Ditto, a wide
variety of combat decks can flourish without Thoughts Betrayed killing
them.

But pretty much all of the *rule* changes, as opposed to textual changes
on cards, came about because of a conspiracy of multiple cards and
strategies coming together (or being hosed together). Looking down the
list in 7/7 (and 6/23), the significant rules changes have a lot of
history to them - (D) not over-riding targets but merely indicating a
typically (D) action (which could also be non-directed, if you took the
relevant actions) had a whole host of useful applications, particularly
with toning down bleed decks which would "randomly" bleed cross-table.
(The player's intention may, of course, not be random, but the effect
was generally quite a way outside of the predator-prey dynamic that
Richard Garfield had been trying to establish, IMO.) Equipment being
non-optional was hardly killer, but fixed a wide variety of headaches
(largely involving Writ of Acceptance, as noted). Aggravated damage
fixed a wide range of perceived problems also.

<dropped or streamlined rules>

>Don't forget Close Quarters, a rule from the original Jyhad rulebook
>that was literally never used on even one single card, even though
>Storm Sewers had the exact same effect.

Ooh, there's a rule I'd expunged from my memory. Thanks. :-)

Always useful to have more examples to hand.



Messages.Author: Chris Berger
Messages.Body:
James Coupe wrote:
>
> To be honest, I'd quite like to see 5 normal damage be slightly weaker
> (somehow) than 5 aggravated damage in the situation you describe, but
> there isn't a useful halfway house between the current rules and the
> V:TES rules that I've ever been able to find. (If you can find one,
> please feel free!)
>

I have one idea, though it's not necessarily a serious suggestion.
What if agg damage rules were more like the RPG? In the RPG,
aggravated damage can only be prevented by fortitude (or similar
effects), rather than being "Soaked" (in the RPG, Soak rolls are
automatically given to every vampire, based on their Stamina, though it
is cool that the card Soak retains this distinction between agg and
non-agg damage). In addition, aggravated wounds cannot be healed
normally (i.e. by burning blood), but have to heal "naturally" taking a
lot of time. It's been a while since I've played the RPG, so forgive
me if this isn't exactly correct - it's at least close.

With current agg-damage rules, the first point of (unprevented) agg
damage is very strong. It sends the opposing vamp to torpor. The
second (and subsequent, up to X+1, where X is the blood on the vamp)
point of agg damage is much weaker - just the same as normal damage.
The X+2 (th) point of agg damage is again very strong, as it burns the
vampire. There seems to be some inconguity here. In the RPG, many
strike effects are agg that are not agg in the card game, because while
those strike effects are supposed to be powerful, they're not supposed
to immediately put the other vampire out of commission if even 1 point
isn't prevented.

Again, this isn't a serious suggestion, just kind of a thought
experiment. I definitely don't expect this to be implemented, and
wouldn't even think of *wanting* it to be implemented until some more
thought and/or testing was put into it. In any case, it would almost
turn VTES into a completely different game, at least combat-wise...
What if aggravated damage reduced a vampire's capacity by X,
permanently (until healed), and also made them burn a blood. This
damage would not immediately send them to torpor. If a vampire takes
more damage than he has blood to burn, he would be sent to torpor
(whether that damage is aggravated or normal). If a vampire takes
aggravated damage when his capacity is 0 (which includes times when he
takes, say, 4 agg when his capacity is only 3), he is burned.

In addition, a vamp with capacity lowered by agg damage would need to
be able to heal the agg. Any one (or possibly all) of these could
work:
a) The vampire takes a +1 stealth action to "heal", removing all
aggravated damage.
b) During your untap phase, spend a pool to completely heal one of your
vampires.
c) Any other vampire may take a +1 stealth action to heal this vampire.
This might require tapping both vampires.

A vampire with 0 capacity might be allowed to "heal" instead of
hunting. Or maybe he's required to hunt anyway, and can only be healed
by some outside help?

Anyway, seems like it'd be interesting, at the very least. Would
severely cripple aggo-poke, and would probably improve decks that seek
to burn vamps with excessive agg-damage. Although, on the whole, it
might weaken combat decks by a fair amount, which IMHO would be bad...

In message <1141006481....@v46g2000cwv.googlegroups.com>, Chris
Berger <ark...@ugcs.caltech.edu> writes:

...

Overall, I really actually quite like this idea. I don't think it'd
work integrating it into the game now, wholesale, but it's really cute.

I think it could make an interesting degenerative disease for a combat /
minion mangling Build Your Own Storyline, to see which clan or which
sect can take control of the cure, and which was responsible for setting
it off in the first place.

You know, that sparks a thought involving a storyline in which each
table has five players - one Camarilla, one Sabbat, one Anarch, one
(non-Anarch) Independent and one Laibon. Anyway.

>In the RPG, many
>strike effects are agg that are not agg in the card game, because while
>those strike effects are supposed to be powerful, they're not supposed
>to immediately put the other vampire out of commission if even 1 point
>isn't prevented.

Well, agg in the card game is a largely massive over-simplification of
the RPG. As is torpor in general. Not that I think it's a *bad* over-
simplification. It's just been very, very simplified from the
complexities RPG. Which is about right for a card game, which doesn't
want too many bizarre quirks lurking around. You want the rules to
provide clever interactions, without being too baroque.

>What if aggravated damage reduced a vampire's capacity by X,
>permanently (until healed), and also made them burn a blood. This
>damage would not immediately send them to torpor. If a vampire takes
>more damage than he has blood to burn, he would be sent to torpor
>(whether that damage is aggravated or normal). If a vampire takes
>aggravated damage when his capacity is 0 (which includes times when he
>takes, say, 4 agg when his capacity is only 3), he is burned.

There's a couple of problems here, mostly practical rather than
theoretical.

One (very minor) problem is that a vampire's capacity can't hit zero in
the card game. Some random loon of no consequence had a bizarre
discussion with LSJ about capacities hitting zero (or negative) shortly
after a rules change to prevent that happening. Read all about it here:
<http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/8fcf02
d82ddadf55>

****
> I have a [1-cap vamp attempts Purity of the Beast, blocked by
> Violet who reduces his capacity to zero while he continues the action
> with Form of Mist, so winds up at -1 capacity.]
> Would that be possible, under the old rules? And can I claim "Stupid
> Interaction of Cards of the Month"?

Yeah :-).

Another way (under the old rules): have a vamp whose capacity is
increased by a few skill cards played by another Meth. Then have that
vampire be reduced to 1 capacity by whatever effects (Violet,
Purity, Child Mind, or IC Wrath), then let the Meth who controls the
skill cards get ousted.

(With the current rules, the vampire would simply be left at 1
capacity).
****

Secondly, you have a lot of overhead here. Keeping track of capacity
reductions is a pain. A better - but equivalent? - way of tracking it
might be to have "wound" counters which count against a vampire's
capacity. Whenever a vampire has more wound counters than capacity
(e.g. 8 on Gitane St Clair), they burn. Wound counters bump off blood.
(Ever play Mage: The Ascension? The same deal as there, with Paradox
bumping off Quintessence on the 20 dot wheel you keep track of them on.)

Wound counters would then be burnable using actions, and card text in
the game could trivially interfere with wound counters. Obeah cards
that suddenly removed all of them, Thanatosis Necrotic Infection cards
that prevented wound counters being burned, Setites with some sort of
Comforting Lure that turns wounds into Corruption counters, and so on.
Easier to interact with than "capacity reduction due to aggravated
damage", and more evocative too. Also potentially more funny, when
Fortitude cards could (say) let you keep working with too many wound
counters, so you suddenly get Rufina Soledad (who really is Stephanie
Beecham, you know) with 4 Enduring Stamina cards on her which let her
treat her capacity as three higher when determining if she burns from
her wounds.

Additionally, 2 aggravated damage could burn a 1 cap - which it can't do
now. So whilst a 1 point agg damage wouldn't burn someone, it could
cause them to do sick and wrong things when hitting multiple points of
agg damage. It's mostly a power increase, which isn't terribly
warranted.

>A vampire with 0 capacity might be allowed to "heal" instead of
>hunting. Or maybe he's required to hunt anyway, and can only be healed
>by some outside help?

Potentially, healing might require blood OR pool e.g. 1 or 2 blood, or 1
pool. If you don't have the blood, you can pay pool to represent some
sort of significant aid.

You might also find in such a game that Trifles or Allies which helped
out here might well be of use.

James Coupe wrote:
>
>
> Secondly, you have a lot of overhead here. Keeping track of capacity
> reductions is a pain. A better - but equivalent? - way of tracking it
> might be to have "wound" counters which count against a vampire's
> capacity. Whenever a vampire has more wound counters than capacity
> (e.g. 8 on Gitane St Clair), they burn. Wound counters bump off blood.
> (Ever play Mage: The Ascension? The same deal as there, with Paradox
> bumping off Quintessence on the 20 dot wheel you keep track of them on.)
>

I do like the idea of wound counters. I was planning on keeping track
of agg-damage reductions in capacity with other-colored counters, and
the idea of getting rid of the capacity-reducing aspect altogether is
probably even better. Each point of aggravated damage = 1 wound
counter. Blood + wound counters cannot be greater than capacity (extra
blood drains off). A vampire with wound counters > capacity is burned.
The only question left is: does a vampire burn blood when he takes
aggravated damage? If not, suddenly agg damage is not necessarily
better than normal damage. So I think a vampire would have to burn a
blood to agg damage to "prevent destruction".

> Wound counters would then be burnable using actions, and card text in
> the game could trivially interfere with wound counters. Obeah cards
> that suddenly removed all of them, Thanatosis Necrotic Infection cards
> that prevented wound counters being burned, Setites with some sort of
> Comforting Lure that turns wounds into Corruption counters, and so on.
> Easier to interact with than "capacity reduction due to aggravated
> damage", and more evocative too. Also potentially more funny, when
> Fortitude cards could (say) let you keep working with too many wound
> counters, so you suddenly get Rufina Soledad (who really is Stephanie
> Beecham, you know) with 4 Enduring Stamina cards on her which let her
> treat her capacity as three higher when determining if she burns from
> her wounds.
>

If someone were to set up a Create-Your-Own Storyline tournament using
these agg rules, I think you would have to add rules to existing card
(like, Restoration also removes 1 wound counter; Renewed Vigor (for)
lets you ignore 1 wound while it's on you, Renewed Vigor (OBE) removes
all wound counters, etc...) . Although I suppose you could also make
library cards that could be printed out and kept in a sleave in front
of regular cards.

>
> Additionally, 2 aggravated damage could burn a 1 cap - which it can't do
> now. So whilst a 1 point agg damage wouldn't burn someone, it could
> cause them to do sick and wrong things when hitting multiple points of
> agg damage. It's mostly a power increase, which isn't terribly
> warranted.
>

Well, it's a power increase for multiple points of agg, but it's a
power decrease for aggro-poke, which is pretty strong currently.

> >A vampire with 0 capacity might be allowed to "heal" instead of
> >hunting. Or maybe he's required to hunt anyway, and can only be healed
> >by some outside help?
>
> Potentially, healing might require blood OR pool e.g. 1 or 2 blood, or 1
> pool. If you don't have the blood, you can pay pool to represent some
> sort of significant aid.
>

Perhaps it takes an action (either by the wounded vamp or another
vamp), burning 2 wounds for every blood spent or 3 wounds for every
pool spent. Or something like that.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
James Coupe wrote:
> In message <1140970031.7...@t39g2000cwt.googlegroups.com>,
> Chris Berger <ark...@ugcs.caltech.edu> writes:
> >This is very odd. An action requires a discipline and a ready vampire.
> > If the vampire loses the discipline, the action continues, but if the
> >vampire is no longer ready, the action fails.
> >
> >See:
> >http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/e147b20e15c9bde1
> >
> >Umm... care to have a go at explaining that one, James? ;)
>
> One explanation would be that the discipline requirement is not one on
> the action, but one on playing the card.

It is of playing the card, correct. It is also therefore something that
the
action requires (but not necessarily requires for successful
resolution).

See also using Inscription to perform a Cryptic Mission.

Playing CM requires Thaumaturgy. The action requires Thaumaturgy.
The action resolves quite nicely even though the acting vampire does
not have Thaumaturgy.

Or using your Thaumaturgy Discipline card to enable a CM, getting
blocked, Weaknessed (removing the Thaumaturgy), and continuing
from the subsequent round with Form of Mist. The action continues
and resolves (if unblocked) just fine.

> As in <http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/
> 9e7c09bec2e12841>, the difference between requiring Obfuscate to play
> the card and the action itself requiring Obfuscate (when it resolves) is
> pointed at.
>
> So if you fail to meet the requirements of an action when it would
> resolve, it fizzles. But meeting the discipline requirement is one you
> meet when playing the card, and does not apply to the action.
>
> However, that conflicts with the wording of Orb of Ulain:
>
> The ally with this equipment cannot be targeted by (D) actions
> that require Auspex, Chimerstry, Dominate, Presence or
> Serpentis.
>
> This implies that the actions themselves do require disciplines, rather
> than just the play of the card.

No conflict. The action requires the Discipline.
Just like a Sewer Lid requires Potence (and will benefit from Increased
Strength even if the Potence-enabling Hand of Conrad is destroyed
with first strike).

> Another explanation, then, would be that while the action does require
> the discipline, only the "Play / Resolve" check on disciplines is made,
> and not some standing check on whether the minion still meets the
> requirements of the action (such as being out of torpor).

Correct.

> Alternatively again, actions that don't specify "May be played by a
> vampire in torpor" (or whatever) are implicitly saying "(D) [This ready
> minion....]" but such text is taken as read because it is only the
> difference that is usually interesting. This would then fail in the
> same way that Ambush fails if the target untaps during the action and,
> as an extension of that, "(D) This ready Baali...." would fizzle if the
> acting vampire stopped being a Baali somehow[0].

Resolution of an action requires a ready acting minion just as
resolution
of a strike requires a ready striking minion.

The action to burn a building with Bomb requires a Bomb at resolution
just
as the strike to inflict 5R damage with a Bomb requires a Bomb at
resolution.
